What the original study did not say

Smiling with a pen in your mouth

A 1988 experiment said forcing a smile makes cartoons funnier. Seventeen laboratories could not confirm it.

In 1988, Fritz Strack and colleagues asked people to hold a pen between their teeth, which forces a smile-like expression, or between their lips, which prevents one. Holding the pen this way, they rated some cartoons. Those who were "smiling" found them funnier. It was evidence for the facial feedback hypothesis: expression influences emotion.

The replication

In 2016, seventeen laboratories repeated the experiment using the same method, agreed in advance with Strack himself. Overall, they found no effect. Strack pointed out differences, such as participants being filmed.

In 2022, a large international study found a small effect when people directly mimicked a smile, but not with the pen. Today it is thought that expressions may influence how we feel a little, but much less than was claimed. "Smile and you will be happy" is an exaggeration.

References

  1. Strack, F., Martin, L. L. y Stepper, S. (1988). Inhibiting and facilitating conditions of the human smile. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 54(5), 768–777.
  2. Wagenmakers, E.-J. et al. (2016). Registered Replication Report: Strack, Martin, & Stepper (1988). Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(6), 917–928.
  3. Coles, N. A. et al. (2022). A multi-lab test of the facial feedback hypothesis by the Many Smiles Collaboration. Nature Human Behaviour, 6, 1731–1742.
